I just felt less intensely sad and more 'flat' than usual, but the voice was still talking to me most days and I was still convinced my neighbors were monitoring me.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe the voice you mentioned, what does it say to you, and how often do you hear it?\n\nPatient: It’s a male voice that I hear almost every day, usually coming from right behind my right ear. It constantly tells me that I'm pathetic and that everyone can see what a failure I am. Even when I put on headphones or check around the room, it doesn't stop or go away.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever believed that the voice you hear is real, to the point where you've tried to respond to it or acted on its commands, or do you recognize it as part of your own thoughts?\n\nPatient: It feels completely real and external, not like my own thoughts at all, which is why I've checked the room or put on headphones to try to block it out. It doesn't actually give me commands to do things, but it constantly insults me and tells me I'm a failure.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where the voice stopped or significantly reduced for more than a couple of weeks, or has it been a constant presence since it started?\n\nPatient: It has been a constant presence almost every single day since it first started over a year ago. There have been brief times where the intensity eased up slightly, but it has never actually stopped or gone away completely for weeks at a time.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any other types of hallucinations, such as seeing things that aren't there, or have you had any other persistent beliefs that you know aren't true, like the belief that your neighbors are monitoring you?\n\nPatient: I don't see anything that isn't there, but I am absolutely convinced that my ex-wife and my old supervisor got people in my building and at work to watch and report on me. Even when I try to tell myself it sounds crazy, every sideways glance or whisper just feels like proof they are out to ruin me.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how your beliefs about being monitored and the voice's comments affect your daily life and interactions with others, and do you think these beliefs are true or could they be part of your own thoughts?\n\nPatient: The constant voice and feeling of being watched make me isolate myself from friends and struggle to focus at work because I am always on edge. As for whether it's true, I try to tell myself it sounds crazy, but every whisper or look still feels like real proof, and the voice sounds completely external—right behind my ear—rather than like my own thoughts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where the voice or your beliefs about being monitored directly influenced your behavior or decisions, and did you act on those beliefs in a way that affected your daily life or relationships?\n\nPatient: Just last week, I saw some coworkers whispering and glancing my way, and I became so sure they were monitoring me that I froze up at my desk and couldn't move or speak for several minutes. I ended up putting on my headphones to block out the voice calling me a failure and completely avoided talking to anyone, which just led to another warning about my declining performance. It's exhausting because I feel like I have to completely isolate myself just to survive the workday.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have noticed any significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning that is not directly caused by the voice or your beliefs, such as a lack of interest in activities you used to enjoy or a decrease in your ability to initiate or maintain relationships?\n\nPatient: Yes, completely separate from the voices, I’ve lost all interest in things I used to love like organizing board-game nights or doing photography, and now I just ignore group chats and isolate in my apartment. I constantly feel like I'm \"on mute\" with no energy to maintain relationships, which has led to warnings at my customer service job and neglecting basic chores like cooking and paying bills on time.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where both the voice and your negative beliefs about being monitored stopped or significantly improved at the same time, or do they seem to fluctuate independently of each other?\n\nPatient: No, they don't really fluctuate independently or ever stop; they've gone hand-in-hand as a constant presence for well over a year now. Even during that stretch last summer when my mood felt a bit lighter or flatter, both the voice and the feeling of being watched remained fully active together.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a significant period of time, say a month or more, where you did not have any hallucinations or delusions, and if so, what was happening in your life during that time?\n\nPatient: Before they first started—which was about a year after my divorce—I didn't experience anything like that at all. Even during times when the voice or the paranoia eased up slightly, they have never completely gone away for a month or more.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there have been any times when the voice or your beliefs about being monitored seemed to be directly triggered by your mood, such as feeling more paranoid when you're sad or hearing the voice more clearly when you're anxious?\n\nPatient: On most days, everything just piles on at once—when I’m feeling completely empty and exhausted, the voice and the paranoia are right there tearing me down. However, they aren't strictly triggered by my mood, because even during that stretch last summer when I didn't feel particularly sad, just flat, the voice and the feeling of being monitored were still happening regularly.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where your mood significantly improved, but the hallucinations and delusions, such as the voice and the belief of being monitored, remained unchanged or even worsened?\n\nPatient: Yes, that actually happened during a stretch last summer. Based on the patient's description of persistent hallucinations (a male voice criticizing them), delusions of being monitored, and significant impairment in social and occupational functioning, 'F20.0' remains a strong candidate. The patient's report of feelings of worthlessness, guilt, and a lack of energy and motivation, which have been present for over two years, suggests a depressive component. The mention of a brief period where the patient felt less intensely sad but still experienced hallucinations and delusions, and the fact that these symptoms have been constant for over a year, suggests that 'F32.3' (Severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms) could be a more accurate diagnosis than 'F32.0'. 'F33.1' (Recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe with psychotic symptoms) is also considered due to the patient's history of persistent depressive symptoms and the presence of psychotic symptoms. 'F33.0' is less likely due to the patient's symptoms not meeting the full criteria for a recurrent depressive disorder.", "is_final": false}

It's exhausting because I feel like I have to completely isolate myself just to survive the workday.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have noticed any significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning that is not directly caused by the voice or your beliefs, such as a lack of interest in activities you used to enjoy or a decrease in your ability to initiate or maintain relationships?\n\nPatient: Yes, completely separate from the voices, I’ve lost all interest in things I used to love like organizing board-game nights or doing photography, and now I just ignore group chats and isolate in my apartment. I constantly feel like I'm \"on mute\" with no energy to maintain relationships, which has led to warnings at my customer service job and neglecting basic chores like cooking and paying bills on time.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where both the voice and your negative beliefs about being monitored stopped or significantly improved at the same time, or do they seem to fluctuate independently of each other?\n\nPatient: No, they don't really fluctuate independently or ever stop; they've gone hand-in-hand as a constant presence for well over a year now. Even during that stretch last summer when my mood felt a bit lighter or flatter, both the voice and the feeling of being watched remained fully active together.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a significant period of time, say a month or more, where you did not have any hallucinations or delusions, and if so, what was happening in your life during that time?\n\nPatient: Before they first started—which was about a year after my divorce—I didn't experience anything like that at all. But since they began about a year and a half ago, they have been a constant presence in my life. Even during times when the voice or the paranoia eased up slightly, they have never completely gone away for a month or more.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there have been any times when the voice or your beliefs about being monitored seemed to be directly triggered by your mood, such as feeling more paranoid when you're sad or hearing the voice more clearly when you're anxious?\n\nPatient: On most days, everything just piles on at once—when I’m feeling completely empty and exhausted, the voice and the paranoia are right there tearing me down. However, they aren't strictly triggered by my mood, because even during that stretch last summer when I didn't feel particularly sad, just flat, the voice and the feeling of being monitored were still happening regularly.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where your mood significantly improved, but the hallucinations and delusions, such as the voice and the belief of being monitored, remained unchanged or even worsened?\n\nPatient: Yes, that actually happened during a stretch last summer. I didn't feel especially sad—just kind of flat—but the voice was still talking to me most days and I was still convinced my neighbors were reporting on me, even though my mood wasn't as low as usual.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if, during that period last summer when your mood felt a bit lighter, the voice and your paranoid beliefs changed in any way, such as becoming less frequent or less intense, or did they remain the same?\n\nPatient: No, they didn't really change or lessen at all during that time. Even though my mood felt more flat than sad, the voice was still talking to me most days and I remained completely certain that my neighbors were reporting on me.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instance where the content of the voice or your beliefs about being monitored directly reflected your current mood or emotional state, such as the voice being more critical when you're feeling down?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are definitely linked. When I'm feeling at my absolute lowest and most exhausted, the voice gets much more critical, calling me pathetic and a failure. In those dark moments, my feelings of worthlessness make me feel like I actually deserve to be watched and punished.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are times when the voice's comments or your beliefs about being monitored seem to directly mirror or exacerbate your current emotional state, such as feeling more criticized by the voice when you're already feeling down?\n\nPatient: Yes, they definitely feed into each other and happen at the same time. On the days when I'm feeling completely empty, exhausted, and down, that's exactly when the voice tears me down the most and I feel most intensely that people are watching and judging me. It all just piles on at once, and it's completely overwhelming.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when the voice's criticism or your beliefs about being monitored seemed to be at odds with your current mood, rather than mirroring or exacerbating it?\n\nPatient: Yes, that goes back to last summer when my mood wasn't actually that low or sad, just kind of flat. Even though I didn't feel deeply depressed, the voice was still talking to me most days and I was still completely convinced my neighbors were monitoring and reporting on me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the voice you hear and your beliefs about being monitored have ever completely disappeared for a period, or have they always been present to some degree since they first started?\n\nPatient: No, they have never completely disappeared since they first started over a year ago. Even during times when they've eased up a little bit, like last summer, the voice and the feeling of being monitored have always been present to some degree.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any periods where you experienced significant depressive symptoms, such as feelings of worthlessness or guilt, that were not directly related to the voice's comments or your beliefs about being monitored?\n\nPatient: Yes, those heavy feelings of hopelessness and worthlessness have been constant ever since my divorce. Even when the voice or the paranoia eased up a bit, I still felt like a complete failure who ruined my ex's life, let my coworkers down, and became a burden to everyone. Those feelings of guilt feel deeply tied to my life falling apart, completely independent of the voice.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any specific events or situations that trigger these intense feelings of guilt and worthlessness, and how they relate to your current life situation?\n\nPatient: Thinking about the divorce and how badly I'm struggling now is what usually triggers it. I constantly feel like I ruined my ex-wife's life, let my supervisor and coworkers down with my failing performance, and even caused the tension between my parents. I just feel like a useless burden who screws up everything and deserves to be punished.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there have been any times when you've experienced hallucinations or delusions without also feeling depressed or having a low mood, or do they always seem to occur together?"

Yes, there was a stretch last summer where I didn't feel especially sad or depressed, just kind of flat. But even without the low mood, the voice was still talking to me most days and I was still convinced my neighbors were monitoring and reporting on me.

A few months after that transition, my drive and energy just completely drained away, and it's been like that ever since.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any periods of significant improvement in your mood, energy, or motivation since the onset of these symptoms two and a half years ago, or have they been consistently present?\n\nPatient: The low mood and lack of energy have been consistently there for the vast majority of the last two years. There was a brief period last summer where I didn't feel quite as deeply sad, but I still felt completely flat and unmotivated, and the voice and paranoia were still going strong.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about the brief period last summer when you felt slightly better, was it a significant improvement where you could function normally for a while, or was it more of a slight lift in your mood without much change in your overall functioning?\n\nPatient: It definitely wasn't a return to normal. I just felt less intensely sad and more 'flat' than usual, but the voice was still talking to me most days and I was still convinced my neighbors were monitoring me.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe the voice you mentioned, what does it say to you, and how often do you hear it?\n\nPatient: It’s a male voice that I hear almost every day, usually coming from right behind my right ear. It constantly tells me that I'm pathetic and that everyone can see what a failure I am. Even when I put on headphones or check around the room, it doesn't stop or go away.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever believed that the voice you hear is real, to the point where you've tried to respond to it or acted on its commands, or do you recognize it as part of your own thoughts?\n\nPatient: It feels completely real and external, not like my own thoughts at all, which is why I've checked the room or put on headphones to try to block it out. It doesn't actually give me commands to do things, but it constantly insults me and tells me I'm a failure.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where the voice stopped or significantly reduced for more than a couple of weeks, or has it been a constant presence since it started?\n\nPatient: It has been a constant presence almost every single day since it first started over a year ago. There have been brief times where the intensity eased up slightly, but it has never actually stopped or gone away completely for weeks at a time.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any other types of hallucinations, such as seeing things that aren't there, or have you had any other persistent beliefs that you know aren't true, like the belief that your neighbors are monitoring you?\n\nPatient: I don't see anything that isn't there, but I am absolutely convinced that my ex-wife and my old supervisor got people in my building and at work to watch and report on me. Even when I try to tell myself it sounds crazy, every sideways glance or whisper just feels like proof they are out to ruin me.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how your beliefs about being monitored and the voice's comments affect your daily life and interactions with others, and do you think these beliefs are true or could they be part of your own thoughts?\n\nPatient: The constant voice and feeling of being watched make me isolate myself from friends and struggle to focus at work because I am always on edge. As for whether it's true, I try to tell myself it sounds crazy, but every whisper or look still feels like real proof, and the voice sounds completely external—right behind my ear—rather than like my own thoughts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where the voice or your beliefs about being monitored directly influenced your behavior or decisions, and did you act on those beliefs in a way that affected your daily life or relationships?\n\nPatient: Just last week, I saw some coworkers whispering and glancing my way, and I became so sure they were monitoring me that I froze up at my desk and couldn't move or speak for several minutes. I ended up putting on my headphones to block out the voice calling me a failure and completely avoided talking to anyone, which just led to another warning about my declining performance. It's exhausting because I feel like I have to completely isolate myself just to survive the workday.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have noticed any significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning that is not directly caused by the voice or your beliefs, such as a lack of interest in activities you used to enjoy or a decrease in your ability to initiate or maintain relationships?\n\nPatient: Yes, completely separate from the voices, I’ve lost all interest in things I used to love like organizing board-game nights or doing photography, and now I just ignore group chats and isolate in my apartment. I constantly feel like I'm \"on mute\" with no energy to maintain relationships, which has led to warnings at my customer service job and neglecting basic chores like cooking and paying bills on time.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where both the voice and your negative beliefs about being monitored stopped or significantly improved at the same time, or do they seem to fluctuate independently of each other?\n\nPatient: No, they don't really fluctuate independently or ever stop; they've gone hand-in-hand as a constant presence for well over a year now. Even during that stretch last summer when my mood felt a bit lighter or flatter, both the voice and the feeling of being watched remained fully active together.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a significant period of time, say a month or more, where you did not have any hallucinations or delusions, and if so, what was happening in your life during that time?\n\nPatient: Before they first started—which was about a year after my divorce—I didn't experience anything like that at all. But since they began about a year and a half ago, they have been a constant presence in my life. Even during times when the voice or the paranoia eased up slightly, they have never completely gone away for a month or more.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there have been any times when the voice or your beliefs about being monitored seemed to be directly triggered by your mood, such as feeling more paranoid when you're sad or hearing the voice more clearly when you're anxious?\n\nPatient: On most days, everything just piles on at once—when I’m feeling completely empty and exhausted, the voice and the paranoia are right there tearing me down. However, they aren't strictly triggered by my mood, because even during that stretch last summer when I didn't feel particularly sad, just flat, the voice and the feeling of being monitored were still happening regularly.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where your mood significantly improved, but the hallucinations and delusions, such as the voice and the belief of being monitored, remained unchanged or even worsened?\n\nPatient: Yes, that actually happened during a stretch last summer. I didn't feel especially sad—just kind of flat—but the voice was still talking to me most days and I was still convinced my neighbors were reporting on me, even though my mood wasn't as low as usual.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if, during that period last summer when your mood felt a bit lighter, the voice and your paranoid beliefs changed in any way, such as becoming less frequent or less intense, or did they remain the same?\n\nPatient: No, they didn't really change or lessen at all during that time. Even though my mood felt more flat than sad, the voice was still talking to me most days and I remained completely certain that my neighbors were reporting on me.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instance where the content of the voice or your beliefs about being monitored directly reflected your current mood or emotional state, such as the voice being more critical when you're feeling down?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are definitely linked. Even during times when they've eased up a little bit, like last summer, the voice and the feeling of being monitored have always been present to some degree.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any periods where you experienced significant depressive symptoms, such as feelings of worthlessness or guilt, that were not directly related to the voice's comments or your beliefs about being monitored?\n\nPatient: Yes, those heavy feelings of hopelessness and worthlessness have been constant ever since my divorce. Even when the voice or the paranoia eased up a bit, I still felt like a complete failure who ruined my ex's life, let my coworkers down, and became a burden to everyone. I constantly feel like I'm \"on mute\" with no energy to maintain relationships, which has led to warnings at my customer service job and neglecting basic chores like cooking and paying bills on time.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where both the voice and your negative beliefs about being monitored stopped or significantly improved at the same time, or do they seem to fluctuate independently of each other?\n\nPatient: No, they don't really fluctuate independently or ever stop; they've gone hand-in-hand as a constant presence for well over a year now. Even during that stretch last summer when my mood felt a bit lighter or flatter, both the voice and the feeling of being watched remained fully active together.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a significant period of time, say a month or more, where you did not have any hallucinations or delusions, and if so, what was happening in your life during that time?\n\nPatient: Before they first started—which was about a year after my divorce—I didn't experience anything like that at all. But since they began about a year and a half ago, they have been a constant presence in my life. Even during times when the voice or the paranoia eased up slightly, they have never completely gone away for a month or more.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there have been any times when the voice or your beliefs about being monitored seemed to be directly triggered by your mood, such as feeling more paranoid when you're sad or hearing the voice more clearly when you're anxious?\n\nPatient: On most days, everything just piles on at once—when I’m feeling completely empty and exhausted, the voice and the paranoia are right there tearing me down. However, they aren't strictly triggered by my mood, because even during that stretch last summer when I didn't feel particularly sad, just flat, the voice and the feeling of being monitored were still happening regularly.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where your mood significantly improved, but the hallucinations and delusions, such as the voice and the belief of being monitored, remained unchanged or even worsened?\n\nPatient: Yes, that actually happened during a stretch last summer. Even though my mood felt more flat than sad, the voice was still talking to me most days and I remained completely certain that my neighbors were reporting on me.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instance where the content of the voice or your beliefs about being monitored directly reflected your current mood or emotional state, such as the voice being more critical when you're feeling down?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are definitely linked. In those dark moments, my feelings of worthlessness make me feel like I actually deserve to be watched and punished.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are times when the voice's comments or your beliefs about being monitored seem to directly mirror or exacerbate your current emotional state, such as feeling more criticized by the voice when you're already feeling down?\n\nPatient: Yes, they definitely feed into each other and happen at the same time. Even during times when the paranoia or voices eased up a bit, that heavy, drained feeling of depression always remained.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when your depressive symptoms, such as feelings of worthlessness or guilt, seemed to improve or worsen independently of the voice's comments or your beliefs about being monitored?"
